10. Concepts as categories

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-10-harmonise.Rmd
book-10-harmonise.Rmd

What you will learn

Use translated concept answers, distinguish recodes from column renames, and harmonise two different site vocabularies.

This chapter uses the synthetic questionnaire dataset described in Getting started. You need: the packages and the matching practice connection described in Before you start. Run the sections in order in one R session. All printed results below were computed with dsOMOP and dsOMOPClient 2.10.5. They are teaching data, not clinical findings.

Concept selections refer to the searches and saved definitions in chapter 4, including the separate questionnaire catalogue. Additional body-measurement concepts are found on screen in the formula walkthrough.

Start this chapter

Start a fresh R session in the book-work directory created in Getting started. Run this setup first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
source("tools/book/display.R")
source("tools/book/fixture.R")
practice <- book_fixture(categories = TRUE)
conns <- practice$conns
names(conns)
#> [1] "site"

The site connection is ready. This chapter creates its temporary questionnaire dataset locally.

Translation follows the value type

A concept-valued answer is a category, not a quantity to average. With the recipe API, the declared value column supplies that type. Your variable name does not need the suffix _concept_id.

education <- omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900001L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"))
class(education)
#> [1] "omop_variable" "list"

The event selects the education question; the reducer reads its last coded answer. Selecting the question concept as the value would answer a different question.

categories <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = education),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(categories, out = c(people = "D_categories"), conns = conns))
#>         people 
#> "D_categories"

Translation is the default. The data values become labelled factors on the server.

ds.omop.table("D_categories", "education", conns = conns)
#> D_categories$education
#>  Secondary education University education 
#>                    6                    6

You see category names and released counts. The concept IDs used in the definition are vocabulary identifiers; they do not appear as numeric answers in this table.

Recode answers to yes and no

An explicit label map changes categories by concept identity. It does not search for text in each site’s database.

fever <- omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900002L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"),
  labels = c("900301" = "yes", "900302" = "no"))
class(fever)
#> [1] "omop_variable" "list"

Only the declared answer concepts receive those labels. A missing answer stays missing; absence of a record is not a clinical “no”.

answers <- omop_recipe(variables = list(fever = fever),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(answers, out = c(people = "D_category_answers"), conns = conns))
#>               people 
#> "D_category_answers"
recode_table_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_category_answers$fever", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
knitr::kable(book_counts(recode_table_result))
Category Count
yes 6
no 6

Full aggregate response

recode_table_result
#> $output.list
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_row.props
#>                         study
#> D_category_answers$fever site
#>                      yes    1
#>                      no     1
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_col.props
#>                         study
#> D_category_answers$fever site
#>                      yes  0.5
#>                      no   0.5
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLE_rvar.by.study_counts
#>                         study
#> D_category_answers$fever site
#>                      yes    6
#>                      no     6
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_proportions
#> D_category_answers$fever
#> yes  no 
#> 0.5 0.5 
#> 
#> $output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_category_answers$fever
#> yes  no 
#>   6   6 
#> 
#> 
#> $validity.message
#> [1] "Data in all studies were valid"

This real ds.table call excludes missing answers and shows the supplied labels. ds.omop.table() additionally retains the complete published category contract, including declared zero levels, and handles punctuation in labels.

Rename the column separately

A column name identifies the variable; a label names one of its categories. Name an explicit variable in the recipe list, without changing what its answers mean.

renamed <- omop_recipe(variables = list(schooling = education),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(renamed, out = c(people = "D_renamed_categories"), conns = conns))
#>                 people 
#> "D_renamed_categories"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_renamed_categories", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id" "schooling"

The list name supplies the scalar variable name. A concept label map would instead change values inside that column. The visit walkthrough uses a value-preserving mutate alias when adding a new name to an already assigned date column.

ds.omop.table("D_renamed_categories", "schooling", conns = conns)
#> D_renamed_categories$schooling
#>  Secondary education University education 
#>                    6                    6

The education categories and counts are unchanged. Next we address differences between sites, where even the vocabulary names can vary.

Rename automatically generated concept columns

Some layouts expand one event into separate columns for each concept. A panel of inpatient/outpatient counts is one example. column_names targets their stable generated keys, not the explicit scalar variable from the previous step.

visit_event <- omop_event("visit_occurrence", c(9201L, 9202L), name = "visits")
visit_population <- omop_population("visitors", index = omop_index(visit_event))
renamed_panel <- omop_recipe(events = list(visit_event),
  populations = list(visit_population),
  column_names = c(visits_9201_count = "admissions", visits_9202_count = "outpatient"),
  outputs = omop_output("panel", rows = "visitors", format = "person_period",
    options = list(sources = list(visit_event), bins = list(width = 30L),
      window = omop_window(0, 29), analyses = "count")))
class(renamed_panel)
#> [1] "omop_recipe" "list"

The keys combine the source name, concept identity and analysis. They remain stable when a vocabulary changes its wording; your chosen column names remain readable. An explicit name cannot collide with a protected or another final column.

book_symbols(recipe_execute(renamed_panel, out = c(panel = "D_renamed_panel"), conns = conns))
#>             panel 
#> "D_renamed_panel"
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_renamed_panel", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "row_id"            "cohort_row_id"     "person_id"         "period_start_days"
#> [5] "period_end_days"   "days"              "admissions"        "outpatient"

The resulting count columns have your declared names. Using column_names with an explicit scalar name such as education would not rename that scalar column.

Find and save the category identities

For the next examples, the questionnaire helper includes a small synthetic classification catalogue. Its teaching ATC and ICD-10 entries illustrate the hierarchy structure; they are not clinical mappings to reuse in a study. Search the catalogue before choosing an order or a rollup.

catalogue <- ds.omop.concept.search(NULL, standard_only = FALSE, limit = 100,
  conns = conns)$pooled
knitr::kable(catalogue[c("concept_name", "vocabulary_id", "concept_class_id", "standard_concept")])
concept_name vocabulary_id concept_class_id standard_concept
Education question Fixture Fixture S
Fever question Fixture Fixture S
Secondary education Fixture Fixture S
University education Fixture Fixture S
Myocardial infarction Fixture Fixture S
Pneumonia Fixture Fixture S
Yes Fixture Fixture S
FEMALE Gender Gender S
MALE Gender Gender S
No Fixture Fixture S
Inpatient Visit Fixture Fixture S
Outpatient Visit Fixture Fixture S
Education answer Fixture Fixture S
Practice medicine Fixture Fixture S
Practice measurement Fixture Fixture S
kilogram Fixture Fixture S
Primary education Fixture Fixture S
English language Language Language S
Teaching ATC first level ATC ATC 1st C
Teaching ATC second level ATC ATC 2nd C
Teaching circulatory code ICD10 ICD10 Hierarchy NA
Teaching respiratory code ICD10 ICD10 Hierarchy NA
Teaching circulatory chapter ICD10 ICD10 Chapter C
Teaching respiratory chapter ICD10 ICD10 Chapter C 
ids <- setNames(catalogue$concept_id, catalogue$concept_name)
education_ids <- ids[c("Primary education", "Secondary education", "University education")]
education_keys <- paste0("concept:", education_ids)
education_set <- omop_concept_set(unname(education_ids))
category_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(list(answers = education_set), category_file)
identical(readRDS(category_file)$answers, education_set)
#> [1] TRUE

The question and answer concepts were located in observation in chapter 4. Primary education is declared in this catalogue but is not an observed answer. A complete public category domain can include an unused level.

Put primary, secondary and tertiary in order

Alphabetical order is not educational order. Declare stable concept identities, then give the three levels the short labels used by the study.

education_ordered <- omop_category(education, omop_category_spec(
  levels = education_keys, order = omop_category_order(education_keys), ordered = TRUE))
ordered_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = education_ordered),
  labels = setNames(c("primary", "secondary", "tertiary"), education_ids))
ordered_result <- recipe_execute(ordered_recipe, out = "D_ordered", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_ordered", "education", conns = conns)
#> D_ordered$education
#>   primary secondary  tertiary 
#>         0         6         6

The table follows primary < secondary < tertiary, including the declared zero level. The ordering is a protocol assertion, not a rank inferred from frequency. Ordered factors use polynomial contrasts; set ordered = FALSE if your model needs nominal treatment contrasts instead. A treatment reference and display order are separate choices.

Exercise. Check the actual type of this column.

Solution: an ordered category

dsBaseClient::ds.class("D_ordered$education", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "dsomop_category_factor" "ordered"                "factor"

It is an ordered factor, not the integers used internally to store a factor.

Choose labels and language

name displays the concept name. code_name adds its vocabulary code; it does not expose numeric concept IDs as answers. A language declaration requests the vocabulary’s synonyms for that language, falling back to a concept name when none is available. It does not translate free text automatically.

language_id <- ids[["English language"]]
styled <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  code_and_name = omop_category(education, omop_category_spec(label_style = "code_name")),
  local_name = omop_category(education, omop_category_spec(
    language = omop_category_language(language_id)))))
style_result <- recipe_execute(styled, out = "D_styled", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_styled", "local_name", conns = conns)
#> D_styled$local_name
#> Secondary schooling  Tertiary schooling 
#>                   6                   6

The teaching vocabulary supplies “Secondary schooling” and “Tertiary schooling” as English synonyms. The category identity is unchanged by these labels.

Exercise. Display the code-and-name variant from the same extraction.

Solution: a second label style

ds.omop.table("D_styled", "code_and_name", conns = conns)
#> D_styled$code_and_name
#> secondary - Secondary education tertiary - University education 
#>                               6                               6

Use code or vocabulary_code when that public coding context is needed. source_code is refused on this route because source-code disclosure needs a separately admitted policy. Prefer names for an ordinary analysis table.

Keep Missing and Unknown distinct

Missing means there is no usable value; Unknown represents OMOP concept zero. Neither means a recorded “no”. The missing policy can make each an explicit factor level without inventing a clinical answer.

missing_recipe <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  education = omop_category(education, omop_category_spec(
    missing = omop_category_missing(na = "level", unknown = "level"))),
  sex = omop_category(omop_variable(name = "sex", table = "person", column = "gender_concept_id"), omop_category_spec(
    missing = omop_category_missing(na = "level", unknown = "level")))))
missing_result <- recipe_execute(missing_recipe, out = "D_missing_categories", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_missing_categories", "education", conns = conns)
#> D_missing_categories$education
#>  Secondary education University education              Missing              Unknown 
#>                    6                    6                   12                    0

Missing answers are now visible as Missing. The public Unknown level may have zero count; declaring it does not assert that anyone has an unknown answer. The sex column contains FEMALE and MALE; its declared Missing and Unknown levels remain empty.

Exercise. Check which declared sex levels are actually observed.

Solution: declared and observed levels

ds.omop.table("D_missing_categories", "sex", conns = conns)
#> D_missing_categories$sex
#>    MALE  FEMALE Missing Unknown 
#>      12      12       0       0

The two observed levels each contain twelve people. A declared Unknown level does not turn an observed FEMALE or MALE value into an unknown value.

Present a semantic flag as an integer, logical or factor

A binary reducer asks whether an event occurred. It has false/true meaning before presentation, so it can safely become 0/1, FALSE/TRUE or named categories.

has_visit <- omop_variable(event = visit_event, reducer = omop_reduce("binary"))
flags <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  integer_flag = has_visit,
  logical_flag = omop_category(has_visit, omop_category_spec(binary = omop_category_binary("logical"))),
  named_flag = omop_category(has_visit, omop_category_spec(binary = omop_category_binary("factor")))))
flag_result <- recipe_execute(flags, out = "D_flags", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_flags", "named_flag", conns = conns)
#> D_flags$named_flag
#>  no yes 
#>   6  18

This “no” means no selected visit in the defined history. It does not mean a negative answer to the fever question. Binary presentation is for semantic flags, not an arbitrary two-level concept column.

Exercise. Inspect the published types without reading patient rows.

Solution: three representations

flag_columns <- recipe_codebook(flag_result)[[1]]$columns
knitr::kable(flag_columns[c("name", "r_type")])
name r_type
person_id character
integer_flag integer
logical_flag logical
named_flag factor

Roll up drug classes and cause chapters

A rollup follows vocabulary relationships. ATC levels are classification classes, not a number of ancestor steps. ICD-10 chapters require the source coding relationships; a similar-looking code prefix is insufficient.

drug_id <- ids[["Practice medicine"]]
knitr::kable(ds.omop.concept.ancestors(drug_id, conns = conns)$pooled)
direction concept_id concept_name domain_id vocabulary_id min_levels_of_separation max_levels_of_separation
ancestor 960001 Teaching ATC first level Drug ATC 2 2
ancestor 960002 Teaching ATC second level Drug ATC 1 1 
icd_id <- ids[["Teaching circulatory code"]]
knitr::kable(ds.omop.concept.relationships(icd_id, relationship_id = "Maps to", conns = conns)$pooled)
direction concept_id relationship_id related_concept_id related_concept_name invalid_reason
forward 960010 Maps to 900201 Myocardial infarction NA 
knitr::kable(ds.omop.concept.relationships(icd_id, relationship_id = "Is a", conns = conns)$pooled)
direction concept_id relationship_id related_concept_id related_concept_name invalid_reason
forward 960010 Is a 960020 Teaching circulatory chapter NA 
knitr::kable(ds.omop.concept.locate(c(drug_id, ids[["Myocardial infarction"]]),
  scope = "pooled", conns = conns)$pooled)
concept_id table_name concept_column n_records n_persons
900201 death cause_concept_id 10 10
950001 drug_exposure drug_concept_id 15 15 
classification_sets <- list(drug = omop_concept_set(drug_id),
  causes = omop_concept_set(unname(ids[c("Myocardial infarction", "Pneumonia")])))
saveRDS(classification_sets, category_file)

Now choose the public domain to be classified. Ambiguous targets fail by default; resolve them in the study protocol with explicit priority or multiple membership. Do not resolve ambiguity by inspecting patient frequencies.

drug_value <- omop_category_reduce(
  omop_category_rows(omop_event("drug_exposure", classification_sets$drug), "concept_id"),
  omop_reduce("last_value"))
cause_value <- omop_category_reduce(
  omop_category_rows(omop_event("death"), "concept_id"), omop_reduce("first_value"))
rollups <- omop_recipe(variables = list(
  atc_first = omop_category(drug_value, omop_category_spec(rollup =
    omop_category_rollup("atc", level = 1, domain = classification_sets$drug))),
  atc_second = omop_category(drug_value, omop_category_spec(rollup =
    omop_category_rollup("atc", level = 2, domain = classification_sets$drug))),
  chapter = omop_category(cause_value, omop_category_spec(rollup =
    omop_category_rollup("icd10", level = "chapter", vocabulary = "ICD10",
      domain = classification_sets$causes)))))
rollup_result <- recipe_execute(rollups, out = "D_rollups", conns = conns)
ds.omop.table("D_rollups", "chapter", conns = conns)
#> D_rollups$chapter
#> Teaching circulatory chapter Teaching respiratory chapter 
#>                           12                            6

The cause counts are now grouped by the synthetic chapter relationships. The underlying person roster is unchanged. Use a validated clinical vocabulary for a real cause-of-death classification.

Exercise. Compare the two ATC levels in the public codebook.

Solution: levels come from vocabulary classes

rollup_columns <- recipe_codebook(rollup_result)[[1]]$columns
lapply(rollup_columns$levels[match(c("atc_first", "atc_second"), rollup_columns$name)],
  function(x) x$labels)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "Teaching ATC first level"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "Teaching ATC second level"

The first and second levels have different labels even though the same drug records contribute to both. Neither level is selected by counting observed drugs.

Read the codebook of each table

Keep the execution result: it carries the admitted table metadata. Calling recipe_codebook() on it is local and does not query patient rows. Calling it on the recipe instead produces a prospective schema, with unresolved fields marked explicitly.

book <- recipe_codebook(ordered_result)
print(book[[1]][c("status", "row_grain", "row_keys")])
#> $status
#> [1] "published"
#> 
#> $row_grain
#> [1] "person"
#> 
#> $row_keys
#> [1] "person_id"
knitr::kable(book[[1]]$columns[c("stable_key", "name", "semantic_type", "r_type",
  "unit", "privacy_class", "missing_policy")])
stable_key name semantic_type r_type unit privacy_class missing_policy
person_id person_id key character not_applicable 1 Ordinary available NA follows the declaration; unavailable and undefined anchors remain NA
education education category ordered_factor not_applicable 3 Ordinary available NA follows the declaration; unavailable and undefined anchors remain NA

The stable key identifies the column before a display rename. Semantic type tells you what a value means; R type tells you how it is represented. Units, category levels, ordering, reference, contrasts and derivation belong with the analysis protocol. None of these fields is a count or a missingness estimate.

Open two practice connections

The other lessons use one server. This check uses two DSLite connections. Both synthetic databases hold the same answer IDs. The second vocabulary calls University education “University qualification” and declares a newer vocabulary version. No patient records are downloaded.

ds.omop.disconnect(conns = conns)
DSI::datashield.logout(conns)
pair <- book_fixture(two_sites = TRUE)
two_conns <- pair$conns
names(two_conns)
#> [1] "site"  "site2"

Each name represents a separate DataSHIELD session with its own private table.

See the vocabulary difference 

lookup <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(900102L, conns = two_conns)
lapply(lookup$per_site, function(x) x["concept_name"])
#> $site
#>           concept_name
#> 1 University education
#> 
#> $site2
#>               concept_name
#> 1 University qualification

This is permitted vocabulary metadata, not observed answer frequencies.

Declare a shared label 

harmonised <- omop_recipe(variables = list(education = omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900001L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"),
  labels = c("900102" = "University education"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
book_symbols(recipe_execute(harmonised, out = c(people = "D_shared"), conns = two_conns))
#>     people 
#> "D_shared"

A common explicit label resolves the known wording difference. Harmonisation is based on concept identity and the published label contract, not on matching patient records or guessing that similar words mean the same thing.

Compare released category sets 

site_tables <- lapply(names(two_conns), function(site)
  ds.omop.table("D_shared", "education", conns = two_conns[site]))
names(site_tables) <- names(two_conns)
site_tables
#> $site
#> D_shared$education
#>  Secondary education University education 
#>                    6                    6 
#> 
#> $site2
#> D_shared$education
#>  Secondary education University education 
#>                    6                    6
identical(dimnames(site_tables[[1]]), dimnames(site_tables[[2]]))
#> [1] TRUE

Both real executions returned the same category set. Now combine their counts:

ds.omop.table("D_shared", "education", conns = two_conns)
#> D_shared$education
#>  Secondary education University education 
#>                   12                   12

The pooled counts add released cells. They do not link people across sites. In a real network, confirm the concept meanings as well as their labels.

Try it

Confirm that the shared definition is a recipe, then close both temporary connections.

Solution

class(harmonised)
#> [1] "omop_recipe" "list"
ds.omop.disconnect(conns = two_conns)
DSI::datashield.logout(two_conns)
unlink(pair$path)

Exercise 2: a common variant

Does a label map change a concept set? Inspect the recipe object locally, compare its selection with the original education variable, and resolve the answer identities using the vocabulary lookup already returned above.

Solution 2

selected <- harmonised$variables$education
without_labels <- selected
without_labels$labels <- NULL
label_ids <- as.integer(names(selected$labels))
answer_names <- lookup$per_site[[1L]]
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Answer = answer_names$concept_name[match(label_ids, answer_names$concept_id)],
  Shared_label = unname(selected$labels)))
Answer Shared_label
University education University education 
identical(selected$event$concepts, education$event$concepts)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(selected$event$concepts, without_labels$event$concepts)
#> [1] TRUE

The label map names the University education answer. Removing that map leaves the observation selection identical (TRUE): it changes the displayed answer label, not which question is selected. Concept meaning still requires study review.

Exercise 3: a pitfall to avoid

Check that the recipe remains serialisable after harmonisation.

Solution 3

is.character(recipe_export_json(harmonised))
#> [1] TRUE

TRUE means this definition can be recorded. It does not prove that two different concepts are clinically equivalent.

Recap

Concept values translate by default. Label maps recode answers; column maps rename variables. Shared labels give common categories across vocabulary wording differences, after you confirm concept meanings.
